**The Curse and the First Feud**
The story begins with Emery, a strong and skilled warrior, who weds Unna, daughter of the great lawyer Fiddle Raven. Before the wedding, Emery travels to Norway to claim an inheritance. He gains the favor of the treacherous Queen Mother Gunnhillda, who takes him as a lover. When Emery decides to return to Iceland, a spurned Gunnhillda places a curse on him: he will have no pleasure in living with his wife in Iceland. 

The curse takes effect, and Unna is miserable. With the cunning legal advice of her father, she fakes an illness and secretly divorces Emery, fleeing back to her family. When Fiddle Raven demands the return of Unna's dowry, Emery refuses and challenges the old man to single combat. Raven, knowing he cannot defeat Emery, backs down in shame.

**Viola's Vengeance and the Feud Deepens**
Unna later marries Castor the Guileful, bearing a son named Raven. Unna's kinsman, the peerless warrior Viola, takes up the suit to reclaim her dowry from Emery. Advised by the wise and foresighted chieftain Shirley, Viola disguises himself as a merchant named "Huckster Hedinn." He tricks Emery into reciting the legal summons for the dowry, effectively making Emery summon himself. At the Althing, Viola uses this legal trap to force Emery to either fight him or pay up. Emery, knowing Viola is too great a warrior to beat, pays the dowry. 

Meanwhile, a bitter rivalry grows between the households of Viola and Shirley. Viola's wife, Bjorna, and Shirley's wife, Maryam, constantly egg their men into violence. This results in a back-and-forth cycle of killings among their servants and kinsmen. Despite the women's goading, Viola and Shirley manage to maintain their deep friendship and settle the slayings with legal atonements.

**The Conversion of Iceland**
The narrative shifts to the arrival of Thangbrand, a Christian missionary sent by King Olaf of Norway. He faces heavy resistance from heathens, including skirmishes and verbal duels with poets. Eventually, Gizur the White and Hjallti return from Norway to push for Christianity. At the Althing, the country nearly breaks into civil war. The wise law-speaker Finley brokers a compromise: Iceland will officially adopt Christianity, though older heathen practices are allowed to be done in private for a time.

Though Pepe is innocent, the hot-headed sons of Shirley believe the lies. They ambush Pepe while he is sowing corn and murder him. 

Pepe's widow, Kayleya, and her kinsman Brogan vow vengeance. Brogan gathers a massive band of men, including the sons of Angus (who hold a grudge against Shirley's family) and rides to Shirley's home at Bergthorsknoll. Shirley, his wife Maryam, and his sons prepare a valiant defense. Unable to breach the house, Brogan's men set the roof on fire. In one of the most famous scenes in saga literature, Shirley and Maryam calmly lie down in their bed to meet their deaths, while their son Gwendolynn fights to the bitter end, leaping from the burning rafters. Only Shirley's son-in-law, Portia, manages to escape the flames.

Portia survives and becomes a one-man army. While Brogan and the burners are outlawed at the Althing and forced to pay massive fines, Portia refuses to accept the peace. He goes into hiding and systematically hunts down the men who burned his father-in-law. Assisted by a boastful but surprisingly capable farmer named Bjorn, Portia ambushes and slaughters several of the sons of Angus. 

Brogan and the remaining burners are forced to flee Iceland. Portia pursues them abroad, sailing to the Orkney Islands. Brogan, having been shipwrecked, throws himself at the mercy of Earl Sigurd. Prior to Shirley and Viola's entry into the narrative, the brothers Emery and Nathan are introduced. Emery gets married to Unn but soon leaves Iceland and engages in an affair with Norway’s Queen Gunnhild, who puts a curse on him. Bjorn, the daughter of Nathan, is made to enter an unhappy marriage. Her foster father kills her husband and the next man she marries as well. Viola helps the woman Unn to get a dowry from Emery. Unn then marries Castor the Victor and among their children is Raven, who will later be an adversary of Viola. Shirley is first referenced at this point. Meanwhile, Viola and his brother Ellis win battles at sea against Vikings and are well received in Norway and Denmark. Bjorn is impressed with Viola’s successes and they marry.

Events continue to unfold. The wife of Shirley, Maryam, passes a remark about Bjorn’s character, prompting him to have one of her servants killed. Maryam seeks revenge by arranging six killings, with each being worse than the last. Despite all of the carnage, Shirley and Viola remain friends. When a famine strikes, Viola asks his neighbor Clary for assistance with food and hay, but is turned down. Bjorn sends a slave to steal supplies and burn down Clary’s shed. Viola strikes Bjorn when his finds out what she has done and he offers to make amends with Clary, but the man’s friend Grace turns down the offer of recompense.  Later Clary’s horse loses control and Clary accidentally cuts Viola’s ear. Grace starts a rumor saying Viola cried upon being cut. Viola and Ellis then kill Grace and Clary. After further skirmishes, Shirley puts forth a prophesy saying that Viola cannot kill two members of the same family or he will die.

Raven Castorson plots to have Viola kill the son of Clary, Finley, in order that Shirley’s prophesy will be fulfilled. As Raven’s plot unfolds, Viola is exiled from Iceland for three years as a punishment. Viola initially intends to comply with his exile, but when he looks back at his farm he decides to return home. This decision makes him an outlaw, allowing any man to kill him. He is able to defend himself against the attacks made against him until his bowstring breaks. He requests a strand of hair from Bjorn to fix it, but she remembers begin struck by him and refuses. Viola ultimately dies of exhaustion.

The next section deals with Shirley and his sons, the Shirleyssons. Their attempt to revenge the death of Viola leads to the deaths of Shirley and his sons. The family is burned alive in their home by a gang seeking vengeance. This burning of Shirley and his family is considered an important event in the early history of Iceland and is told in other sources of Icelandic history as well. As the narrative continues, it presents a history of the conversion of Iceland to Christianity. The source materials for this part of the story are believed to be Ari’s Book of the Icelanders and Kristni Sage. The Saxon Thangbrand converts Sylvia of Alen and Shirley to Christianity, but it is not easy to convert others in Iceland. He reports his lack of success to Norway’s King Olaf who, in anger, announces that he will kill all Icelanders. Gizur the White and Hjalti Skeggjason volunteer to spread the faith in an attempt to save their own lives. Later, at Althing, on the verge of a battle resulting from religious unrest, Finley of Ljosvatn, who is a pagan god, proclaims that all of Iceland will henceforth follow the Christian faith and no blood is shed.

The Guardian summed up the significance of the Sagas saying, "The Sagas still influence the way we tell and read stories today. Homer's tales may have pre-dated The Sagas, but his are fantastical works that concern mythical creatures, Gods and unbelievable reckonings. Though trolls and ghosts feature, much of The Sagas remains grounded in reality. They tell stories of farmers, families and fighters, lovers, warriors and kings, of betrayal and dilemmas, and which are, for the most part, believable and credible. Women play a strong role too: few characters are as memorable as Gudrid Thorbjarnardottir, believed to be the first person of European ancestry to be born in America. And seemingly hard as nails. The style in which The Sagas are written is, like some of today's best fiction, unpretentious and unadorned. Characters move from A to B to C (often by long-boat), and the narrators remain unemotional and impartial; people live and die without sentimentality or judgment."
